full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: The detenu Md Aftab Hossain is under Preventive Detention in Barisal District Jail. The detenu stood arraigned for offence punishable under section 19(a) and (f) of The Arms Act, 1878 in Kotwali Police Station Case No. 30 dated 20-7-2001. On the strength of a petition for bail presented by detenu as accused-petitioner under section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before High Court Division on 20-8-2001 a Rule was issued by High Court Division calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Barisal to show cause as to why the detenu should not be enlarged on bail in Kotwali Police Station Case No. 30 dated 20-7-2001 corresponding to GR No. 357 of 2001 pending in the Court of Magistrate, First Class, Barisal and detenu was, also, enlarged on ad-interim bail for a period of six (6) months on furnishing bail bond to the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner, Barisal or till submission of Police Report whichever is earlier. 

 3. The petitioner, full brother of the Detenu, invoking this Court's power under section 491 of The Code of Criminal Procedure (shortly The Code) challenged the legality of the order of detention of the Detenu on presentation of a petition under section 491 of the Code which has been numbered as Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 6693 of 2001. 

 4. Section 491 of the Code enshrines that if a person within the territorial jurisdiction of the Courts is illegally or improperly detained in public or private custody, the High Court Division may direct that the said detenu be brought before it to be dealt with according to law and he is not being held in detention illegally and unlawfully and be set at liberty. This concept of the freedom of the citizen of the land in case of unlawful detainment, either in prison or private custody, originated from England, by means of writ of habeas corpus ad subjiciendum (that you have the body to submit or answer). Habeas corpus ad subjiciendum is directed to the person who had the prisoner in custody, commanding such person to produce the prisoner in court on cause of detention ad faciendum subjiciendum et recipiendum whatever the court should ordain in that behalf. 

 5. The writ of habeas corpus ad subjiciendum, commonly known as the writ of habeas corpus, is a prerogative process for securing the liberty of the subject by affording an effective means of immediate release from unlawful or unjustifiable detention whether in prison or in private custody. The writ is applicable as a remedy in all cases of wrongful deprivation of personal liberty. The illegal detention of a subject, that is, a detention or imprisonment which is incapable of legal justification, is the basis of jurisdiction in habeas corpus. In any matter involving the liberty of the subject the action of Executive is subject to the supervision and control of the Judges on habeas corpus. Judges are guardians of liberty of the subject. Judges are to see that the wrong is avenged and the wrongdoer is dealt with according to law. The judges owe a duty to safeguard the liberty of the subject. 

 7. The origin of the Writ of habeas corpus is lost in antiquity. It may have antedated Magna Cart a, but it seems that until Magna Carta was assented to by King John, June 15, 1215, and for some time thereafter, various other writs were used for the purpose of enforcing the right of personal liberty. In the course of time the efficiency of the remedy was greatly impaired by certain decisions of the King's Bench Division as to the cases to which writ was applicable. Continued abuses and evasions of the remedy led to the passing of Habeas Corpus Act under which the writ of habeas corpus became the most celebrated writ in English Law. 

 (a) 	The detenu is a marked terrorist and he is alleged to be in possession of illegal arms. A two barrel gun, one barrel gun, fifty-two rounds of cartridges and other weapons were recovered from his residence at Kashipur and Kotwali Police Station. Case No. 30 dated 20-7-2001 under section 19(a) and (f) of The Arms Act, 1878 had been registered against him. 

 (d) 	An Anti corruption Case and a GD Entry had been registered against the detenu. 

 14.	On a reading of the grounds communicated to the detenu it appears that criminal activities of the detenu are relatable to past activities, Kotwali Police Station Case No. 30 dated 20-7-2001, Anticorruption Case without mentioning any Number and a GD Entry noted in Police Station are detenu's alleged past activities. In Kotwali Police Station Case No. 30 dated 20-7-2001 the detenu had been granted ad-interim bail by High Court Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 6002 of 2001 by order dated 20-8-2001. The other grounds canvassed for detention are all vague. It is well established that in a case of Preventive Detention the grounds must be very clear, specific and definite so as to enable the detenu to make an effective representation to the authority to take a view in his favour. True it is that Preventive Detention measure is harsh but it is equally true that it becomes necessary in the larger interest of the society. It is to be kept in view that it is in the nature of a precautionary measure taken for preservation of public order. The power is to be used with utmost caution and circumspection. An order of detention passed upon a citizen on fictitious, vague and indefinite grounds and founded on colourable satisfaction affecting the right of a citizen, and not in the larger interest of the society and public at large must be quashed. 

 20. Corollary thereof is that Criminal Miscellaneous Case stands allowed. Rule is made absolute. The detention of the detenu Md Aftab Hossain, son of Alhaj Amjad Ali is declared as illegal and improper and we record direction that the detenu Md Aftab Hossain, son of Alhaj Amjad Ali now detained in Barisal Jail be set at liberty at once, if not required in any other case.
